items.title: «Biens mal acquis»: Ali Bongo sort du silence et défend la mémoire de son père
items.description: Après plusieurs mois de silence, l’ancien président gabonais Ali Bongo Ondimba a repris la parole, samedi 19 septembre 2026, pour réagir au volet gabonais de l’affaire dite des «biens mal acquis». S’il assure ne pas vouloir intervenir sur le fond de la procédure judiciaire française, il conteste vivement les observations formulées par l’État gabonais, qu’il estime préjudiciables à la mémoire de son père, Omar Bongo Ondimba. Ali Bongo Ondimba a choisi une déclaration vidéo, diffusée samedi 19 septembre 2026 par plusieurs médias, pour sortir de son silence. L’ancien chef de l’État gabonais s’est exprimé sur l’évolution du dossier des «biens mal acquis», particulièrement sur la position récemment défendue par les autorités de Libreville devant la justice française. Dans son intervention, Ali Bongo précise qu’il ne souhaite pas contester le fond de la procédure en cours en France. Il estime que les faits doivent être examinés par la justice et refuse de se substituer aux juridictions saisies. Son désaccord porte plutôt sur les observations formulées par la République gabonaise à l’encontre de son défunt père, Omar Bongo Ondimba. Prenant cette fois la parole comme fils, l’ancien président affirme que ces observations portent atteinte à la mémoire de l’ancien dirigeant gabonais. «Un fils peut accepter que l’on juge l’action politique de son père sans accepter que l’on bafoue sa mémoire», a-t-il déclaré. Cette prise de position intervient quelques semaines après les réquisitions du Parquet national financier (PNF) français. Le 27 juillet 2026, le parquet a requis le renvoi devant le tribunal correctionnel de Paris de 18 personnes et cinq sociétés dans le volet gabonais de l’affaire. Parmi les personnes concernées figurent neuf enfants d’Omar Bongo, dont Pascaline Bongo et Omar Denis Junior. Le patrimoine immobilier concerné est évalué par la justice française à environ 85 millions d’euros. Ali Bongo lui-même ne figure pas parmi les personnes visées par ces réquisitions. L’affaire, engagée en France depuis plusieurs années à la suite notamment des procédures initiées par Transparency International et Sherpa, connaît ainsi une nouvelle étape judiciaire. Les accusations portées dans cette procédure restent soumises à l’appréciation des juridictions françaises et ne valent pas condamnation. Le passé judiciaire du dossier rattrape le débat La sortie d’Ali Bongo a rapidement provoqué des réactions au Gabon. Certains commentateurs ont notamment rappelé que l’État gabonais avait déjà pris part à la procédure alors qu’Ali Bongo était lui-même président de la République. Une archive publiée par Challenges le 14 janvier 2011, sous le titre «Biens mal acquis: le Gabon se constitue partie civile», est notamment revenue au centre des débats. Selon les éléments rapportés à l’époque, Me Patrick Maisonneuve, avocat de l’État gabonais, indiquait que cette décision avait été «décidée par le président Ali Bongo». Cette chronologie est également rappelée dans plusieurs publications parues après la déclaration du 19 septembre. Elle appelle toutefois une distinction importante: la constitution de partie civile de l’État gabonais ne constituait pas, en elle-même, une condamnation d’Omar Bongo ni une reconnaissance de culpabilité. Elle plaçait simplement l’État dans la procédure judiciaire. Les critiques adressées aujourd’hui à Ali Bongo s’appuient néanmoins sur cette séquence. Dans une tribune publiée le 20 septembre par Gabonews, le journaliste-écrivain Maixent Georges Ntoutoume-Ndong parle notamment d’«amnésie sélective», en rappelant que l’État gabonais était entré dans le dossier sous la présidence d’Ali Bongo. D’autres voix ont également réagi. L’éditorialiste Serge Abessolo, cité par Gabon Media Time, a opposé à la défense de la mémoire paternelle avancée par Ali Bongo l’idée que «honorer la mémoire d’un père se traduit dans les actes posés pour la défendre». Une affaire qui dépasse désormais le seul terrain judiciaire Entre la défense de la mémoire d’Omar Bongo par son fils et les rappels concernant les décisions prises sous la présidence d’Ali Bongo, l’affaire des «biens mal acquis» retrouve ainsi une forte dimension politique et mémorielle au Gabon. Le dossier reste toutefois, sur le plan judiciaire, entre les mains de la justice française. Les réquisitions du PNF doivent encore être suivies des décisions des magistrats compétents quant à la tenue éventuelle d'un procès. En sortant du silence le 19 septembre, Ali Bongo a donc rouvert un débat qui dépasse la seule procédure française: celui de la mémoire d’Omar Bongo, de l’héritage de son long règne et des décisions prises par son propre successeur lorsqu’il était encore à la tête du Gabon. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article «Biens mal acquis»: Ali Bongo sort du silence et défend la mémoire de son père est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Founder’s Day: We face forward, but are we moving?
items.description: Today, Ghana observes Founder’s Day, and while many of us will appreciate the chance to rest, spend time with family, attend an event, or simply step away from our normal routines, I find myself wondering what this day is actually asking of us. We can post photographs of Osagyefo Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, repeat his words, dress in our beautiful Ghanaian colors, and speak proudly about the history of our independence. But somewhere between remembrance and celebration, we must also honestly examine what we have done with the freedom, responsibility, and possibilities handed to us. Otherwise, Founder’s Day risks becoming another holiday we celebrate without allowing its meaning to challenge us. I approach this day from an interesting place because I am both American and Ghanaian. I have experienced Ghana from the outside and now from within, and living here has caused me to examine both identities in ways I probably never would have otherwise. I can appreciate what other countries have built without believing Ghana must imitate them, and I can love Ghana without pretending that everything here is working as it should. In fact, I believe loving a country requires enough courage to question it, enough commitment to work for it, and enough honesty to acknowledge when we ourselves are contributing to the problems we complain about. That is what keeps bringing me back to one of Nkrumah’s most enduring declarations: “We face neither East nor West; we face forward.” More than six decades later, those words still demand something from us. Forward was never supposed to mean waiting for someone from the East or West to decide what development should look like for Ghana or Africa. It was not supposed to mean measuring our worth by the amount of foreign funding we could attract or the number of international organizations willing to validate our ideas. Forward required Africans to imagine, build, govern, produce, educate, innovate, and ultimately take responsibility for Africa. This does not mean Ghana should close its doors to international partnerships, foreign investment, development assistance, or knowledge exchange. We live in an interconnected world, and there is tremendous value in genuine partnership. However, partnership and dependency are not the same thing, and we have to become much more intentional about recognizing the difference. Someone contributing a dollar, euro, or pound toward an African initiative should not automatically receive the intellectual authority to determine what our communities need, how our development should proceed, or what success should look like. Financial contribution cannot become a substitute for local knowledge, and generosity should never quietly transform into ownership. Nkrumah told African leaders in 1963 that, the independence of our separate States is meaningless, unless the whole of Africa becomes free and united. His generation fought for political independence, but ours must continue defining what meaningful independence requires in the twenty-first century. What does freedom mean if we export raw materials and import expensive finished products made from those same resources? What does it mean if other people own much of the technology we depend upon, control the platforms through which we communicate, hold the capital our entrepreneurs need, and increasingly collect the data that will shape the next generation of artificial intelligence? Political independence gave us the authority to determine our future. It did not guarantee that we would build the systems necessary to secure it. Our young people are one of the clearest places where that work must happen. We often speak proudly about Africa having one of the youngest populations in the world, but youthfulness by itself is not an achievement. A young population without quality education, opportunity, mentorship, employment, skills, capital, and meaningful pathways toward ownership can quickly become a frustrated one. We cannot continue telling young people they are the leaders of tomorrow while excluding them from meaningful participation today. If we believe they are our future, then our budgets, institutions, schools, businesses, community organizations, and national priorities should demonstrate that belief. There are encouraging efforts underway. Under President John Dramani Mahama’s administration, programs including the National Coders Programme, National Apprenticeship Programme, Adwumawura, and investments in research and innovation are attempting to address parts of this challenge. The 2026 Budget allocated resources to coding and digital skills, apprenticeship training, entrepreneurship, and the Ghana National Research Fund. These investments matter because Ghana cannot talk seriously about competing in a modern global economy while treating research, technical education, entrepreneurship, and digital literacy as optional extras. Yet government programs alone cannot produce the Ghana we want. A coding program can provide technical knowledge, but it cannot manufacture discipline. An entrepreneurship initiative can provide opportunity, but it cannot guarantee integrity. An apprenticeship can teach a trade, but society must still respect skilled work and create an environment in which that person can build a dignified livelihood. Government has responsibilities, certainly, but so do families, educators, businesses, professionals, traditional leaders, religious institutions, civil society organizations, communities, and young people themselves. National development cannot be outsourced to the Presidency. Agriculture presents another test of our seriousness. We have repeated for generations that agriculture is the backbone of Ghana, yet our treatment of farmers does not always reflect the importance we claim they have. The future Ghanaian farmer should not simply be someone working harder with a cutlass. Agriculture must increasingly involve technology, research, irrigation, climate-smart practices, storage, processing, logistics, financing, branding, manufacturing, data, and access to markets. Farming should be an industry in which a young Ghanaian can see intellectual challenge, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the possibility of building wealth. The government’s Feed Ghana Programme and broader agricultural transformation agenda are intended to increase domestic production, improve food security, reduce dependence on imports, and strengthen value addition. Ghana is also pursuing greater local cocoa processing, which raises a question we should have been asking for decades: Why are we satisfied with producing raw materials while other countries create substantially more value from what grows beneath our feet? Cocoa should not leave Ghana as one economic opportunity and return as another country’s finished product, brand, employment opportunity, intellectual property, and profit. The same principle must extend across agriculture and our natural resources if we are serious about building an economy that creates and retains more value at home. Technology presents an even more urgent version of that challenge. As artificial intelligence transforms economies around the world, I keep asking whether Africa intends to help build this technological future or simply become one of its largest markets. There is a significant difference between using AI and participating in the ownership, research, infrastructure, governance, and development of AI. If the platforms are built elsewhere, the computing infrastructure is owned elsewhere, the algorithms are designed elsewhere, the intellectual property is registered elsewhere, and African data helps improve systems whose economic value ultimately accumulates elsewhere, we must ask whether we are creating technological independence or introducing a more sophisticated form of dependency. Our young people therefore need opportunities to do more than use the newest tools. They need opportunities to code, research, engineer, question, design, create, govern, invest, and own. African innovators should also be able to solve African problems without believing that an idea becomes legitimate only after someone outside the continent funds or approves it. International expertise and investment can strengthen what we build, but Africa cannot perpetually be the project while somebody else remains the project manager. This brings me to the government and the role of citizens. I believe President John Dramani Mahama’s administration is doing important work and pursuing policies that deserve serious attention. The 24-Hour Economy initiative seeks to expand productive activity and employment beyond traditional working hours. The Big Push is focused on infrastructure. Feed Ghana is addressing agricultural production and food security. Adwumawura and apprenticeship initiatives focus on entrepreneurship and skills development, while investments in research and digital skills recognize the importance of preparing Ghana for a changing global economy. Efforts to strengthen value-for-money oversight in public expenditure are equally important because development is not simply about how much the government spends; it is about whether citizens receive the value they were promised. Supporting good national policies, however, cannot mean abandoning accountability, just as demanding accountability cannot mean hoping an administration fails because we belong to another political party. Ghana cannot progress if we only want the country to succeed when our preferred party occupies the Presidency. When a government policy fails, ordinary Ghanaians experience the consequences. When public money is wasted, it is Ghanaian opportunity that disappears. When schools underperform, roads deteriorate, businesses struggle, or young people lose hope, our party colors do not insulate us from the consequences. Political competition has its place in a democracy, but our loyalty to political organizations should never become greater than our loyalty to the country those organizations are competing to govern. Accountability must also extend beyond politicians. We regularly ask whether the President, ministers, Members of Parliament, and public officials are doing their jobs, but how often do we turn that same question toward ourselves? Are we doing the work we are paid to do? Are we giving people the service they deserve? Are teachers teaching with commitment? Are contractors building to the standards for which they were paid? Are business owners treating workers fairly? Are public servants actually serving the public? Are professionals mentoring those coming behind them? Are people entrusted with public resources protecting those resources as carefully as they would protect money belonging to their own families? We cannot demand excellence from Ghana while offering mediocrity to Ghana. There is a powerful statement attributed to Nkrumah: “Action without thought is empty. Thought without action is blind.” Whatever sector we apply those words to, the challenge is clear. Ghana does not suffer from a shortage of conferences, committees, reports, launches, panels, workshops, strategic plans, or beautifully written proposals. We have discussed our potential extensively. The evidence of our commitment must ultimately become visible in what changes: a child whose opportunities expand, a farmer whose income increases, a young Ghanaian who develops technology and retains ownership of it, a business that grows and creates employment, a community that becomes cleaner, or an institution that functions properly even when nobody important is watching. For those of us connected to the diaspora, that accountability has another dimension. Ghana cannot simply become the place we love loudly in December. Our relationship with this country must go further than vacations, property ownership, nightlife, investment opportunities, and beautiful declarations about coming home. If we claim Ghana, then Ghana’s challenges belong to us too. Coming home must eventually mean contributing knowledge, building institutions, creating employment, mentoring someone, investing responsibly, supporting communities, transferring skills, or finding some meaningful way to participate in the country’s development. My American identity has given me perspectives and opportunities for which I am grateful, but my Ghanaian identity continually asks what I am doing with them here. Perhaps that is what Founder’s Day should really do to us. It should make us uncomfortable enough to examine what we are founding ourselves. Nkrumah’s life and political legacy will continue to be studied, debated, praised, and criticized, as the lives of consequential leaders should be. Yet whatever position one takes on every aspect of his leadership, it is difficult to ignore the magnitude of the question his generation placed before ours: What will Africans do with African freedom? That question belongs to us now. What will we do with our land, our cocoa, our gold, our intellectual capacity, our culture, our creativity, our technology, our data, and, most importantly, our children? Will we continue waiting for someone else to discover our potential, fund it, validate it, research it, write another report about it, and eventually profit from it? Or will we develop the discipline to transform potential into institutions, products, industries, knowledge, ownership, and opportunities that remain here? So on this Founder’s Day, I am less interested in simply saying “Happy Founder’s Day” than I am in asking what each of us is founding. What are we building that will outlive us? Who are we teaching and mentoring? What problems are we solving? What institutions are we strengthening? What knowledge are we passing forward? What are we willing to contribute when nobody is applauding, funding, photographing, or rewarding us? These are not questions reserved for presidents, ministers, CEOs, or wealthy people. They belong to every citizen who expects Ghana to become something greater. Ghana does not need all hands on deck only when there is something personal or political to gain. Nation-building requires people willing to contribute even when somebody else receives the recognition. It requires citizens who understand that another Ghanaian’s progress does not diminish their own and that strengthening an institution we may eventually leave is still worthwhile because that institution belongs to the country. It requires those who voted for the government and those who did not, those who live here and those who have returned, those with significant resources and those whose contribution may simply begin with doing their own work exceptionally well. Nkrumah said, “We face neither East nor West; we face forward.” The more I reflect on those words, the more I wonder whether the most important word in that sentence is not East, West, or even forward. Perhaps it is we . Ghana will not move forward because one President wants it to, and Africa will not move forward because one generation talks about it. Progress requires the farmer and the programmer, the teacher and the entrepreneur, the government official and the community volunteer, the traditional leader and the young innovator, those living at home and those returning from abroad. Today, we remember those who dreamed of freedom. Tomorrow, we still have to decide what we are going to do with it. If Founder’s Day means anything beyond a day away from work, perhaps it should remind us that responsibility for Ghana did not end with the generation that founded it. They handed that responsibility forward, and now it is in our hands. The question is whether we are prepared to carry it.

items.title: Kiev cherchait à entraîner la Pologne dans la guerre contre la Russie, selon l’ex-vice-Premier ministre polonais
items.description: Le president du parti polonais « Droit et Justice », Jaroslaw Kaczynski, a declare qu'au debut de l'operation militaire speciale en Ukraine, Kiev comptait entraîner la Pologne dans des combats contre la Russie, a rapporte le journal Rzeczpospolita. Kaczynski occupait a l'epoque le poste de vice-Premier ministre de Pologne au sein du gouvernement de Mateusz Morawiecki, ainsi que celui de president de la commission du Conseil des ministres chargee des questions de securite nationale et de defense. Selon lui, au debut du conflit, la partie ukrainienne attendait de Varsovie des mesures que la Pologne ne pouvait pas prendre. Il a souligne qu'a l'epoque, le pays ne disposait pratiquement pas de forces armees. Kaczynski a emis l'hypothese que l'adhesion de la Pologne a l'OTAN avait pu jouer un role dans les calculs de l'Ukraine, notant toutefois qu'il n'en etait pas certain. Cela dit, Varsovie et Kiev parvenaient alors a trouver des solutions aux problemes qui surgissaient entre les deux pays, ce qui permettait de maintenir de bonnes relations entre la Pologne et l'Ukraine Apres le debut du conflit, la Pologne est devenue l'un des principaux allies de l'Ukraine : le pays a accueilli le flux principal de refugies ukrainiens et est egalement devenu la principale plaque tournante pour les livraisons d'armes occidentales a Kiev. Cependant, les relations entre la Pologne et l'Ukraine se sont compliquees ces dernieres annees en raison de divergences, notamment sur les questions de memoire historique. Les tensions se sont particulierement intensifiees en juin dernier apres la decision des autorites ukrainiennes de donner a l'une des unites de leurs forces armees le nom de « Heros de l'UPA », en hommage a l'Armee insurrectionnelle ukrainienne, dont l'heritage est associe aux violences attribuees aux nationalistes ukrainiens contre la population polonaise pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, notamment le massacre de Volhynie , au cours duquel au moins 100 000 Polonais ont ete victimes des militants de l'UPA entre 1943 et 1945. En reponse, le president polonais Karol Nawrocki a dechu Volodymyr Zelensky de la plus haute distinction nationale du pays : l'Ordre de l'Aigle blanc. La Russie denoncait deja depuis 2014 la nature nazie du regime de Kiev et continue de le faire jusqu'a aujourd'hui. Lors de la seance pleniere du Forum economique international de Saint-Petersbourg 2026, le president russe Vladimir Poutine a rappele que l'un des objectifs de l'operation militaire speciale en Ukraine etait la denazification.

items.title: Le Roi exprime ses condoléances à Cheikh Khalifa Ben Zayed Al Nahyane suite au décès d'Ahmed Ben Rached Al-Maktoum
items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI a adressé un message de condoléances et de compassion au Président de l’État des Émirats Arabes Unis, Cheikh Khalifa Ben Zayed Al Nahyane, à la suite du décès d'Ahmed Ben Rached Al-Maktoum. Dans ce message, le Roi affirme avoir appris avec une grande émotion et une profonde affliction le décès d'Ahmed Ben Rached Al-Maktoum, que Dieu l’agrée parmi les vertueux de Ses serviteurs. « Face à cette douloureuse épreuve, la volonté divine étant imparable, Je tiens à exprimer à votre Altesse, et à travers vous, aux proches et à la famille du défunt et au peuple émirati frère, Mes vives condoléances et Mes sincères sentiments de sympathie et de compassion, important le Tout-Puissant de vous accorder patience et réconfort » , souligne le Souverain. Le Roi prie Dieu d’entourer le défunt de Sa Sainte miséricorde et de l’accueillir dans Son vaste paradis et de le rétribuer amplement pour les services louables rendus à sa patrie et à sa nation et pour les bonnes oeuvres qu'il a accomplies. « Tout en partageant votre peine, J'implore le Très-Haut de vous préserver et de perpétuer sur vous les bienfaits de la santé et de la quiétude » , affirme le Souverain, tout en faisant part de Son estime et de Sa considération à Son frère Cheikh Khalifa Ben Zayed Al Nahyane. items.title: Sheenah Naturals unveils Akuaba Collection at Beauty Inside Out Conference
items.description: Ghanaian beauty and wellness brand Sheenah Naturals has unveiled its new premium Akuaba Collection at the Beauty Inside Out Conference, held on Friday, September 18, 2026, at Africa Trade House, 1st Floor, Accra. Founded by Gladys Nana Akua Cobbina, Sheenah Naturals has grown since its establishment in 2018 into a Ghanaian beauty brand offering skincare and hair-care products inspired by natural African ingredients. The Akuaba Collection, inspired by the iconic Ghanaian Akuaba doll, combines African heritage with a modern, premium feel. The unisex collection features luxury body-care products and represents the brand’s ambition to take Ghanaian beauty and African-inspired products to the global market. The launch formed part of the Beauty Inside Out Conference, which brought together women for conversations on beauty, wellness, self-care and purposeful living. Other brands featured at the event included Nunya Naturals and Perfumes by Ayida Jackson, showcasing the growing range of locally developed beauty and wellness products. For Gladys Nana Akua Cobbina and Sheenah Naturals, the Akuaba launch marks another chapter in the evolution of a proudly Ghanaian brand with global ambitions.

items.title: 4 471 licences, 89 journées et 70,8 millions de FCfa de droits d’organisation
items.description: La Fédération sénégalaise de lutte (Fsl) a présenté, le 12 septembre 2026 à l’Arène nationale, le bilan de sa première saison dans sa nouvelle configuration institutionnelle. Le rapport d’activités fait le point sur la saison 2025-2026, marquée par le passage du Cng à la Fsl, avec 4.471 licences délivrées, 89 journées de lutte avec frappe et 70,8 millions de FCfa de droits d’organisation. Il revient également sur les actions menées, les difficultés rencontrées et les priorités pour la prochaine saison. Après une première année d’existence, la nouvelle Fédération sénégalaise de lutte a été confrontée à de nouvelles exigences en matière de gouvernance, de transparence, de professionnalisation et de développement de la discipline. Lutte olympique, beach wrestling, lutte sans frappe et lutte avec frappe ont constitué les principaux axes d’activité, avec un accent particulier sur la formation, le développement régional et la préparation des Joj « Dakar 2026 ». La Fsl a enregistré 4.471 licences au cours de la saison : 3.179 en lutte avec frappe, 1.239 en lutte sans frappe et 53 pour la lutte olympique et le beach wrestling. Ces chiffres confirment le poids de la lutte traditionnelle et soulignent le retard des disciplines olympiques, dont le développement passe par une détection plus large, une formation renforcée et un meilleur accompagnement des jeunes. À Thiès et Ziguinchor, la Fsl a multiplié les entraînements et les stages pour renforcer le niveau technique et préparer la relève. À Dakar, les séances organisées à l’Arène nationale ont toutefois été suspendues en janvier 2026 pour des raisons administratives, affectant la régularité de la préparation. La relance de la lutte olympique figure ainsi parmi les priorités de la prochaine saison, avec l’ambition de renforcer la formation, d’élargir la détection et d’offrir aux athlètes de meilleures conditions de préparation. Par Abdoulaye DEMBÉLÉ

items.title: T-bills: 91-day, 364-day yields to trade slightly higher in second half of 2026
items.description: The 91-day bill is expected to trade within 5.5%-7.5% in the second half of 2026, while the 364-day bill would trade within 12.5%-14.0%. According to Databank Research, its outlook reflects the competing effects of the Treasury’s cost-containment strategy and higher funding requirements linked to upcoming obligations. It said in its 2026 Half-Year Report that active yield management should limit sharp repricing, although increased financing needs are likely to keep rates under moderate upward pressure over the period. Presently, the yields on the 91-day and 364-day bills are hovering around 4.9% and 10% respectively. “We expect domestic liquidity conditions to remain broadly supportive in 2H’26 [second-half 2026], with the GH¢10.8 billion DDEP [Domestic Debt Exchange Programme] coupon payment due in August 2026 providing an initial boost to market liquidity. Reinvestment by banks, pension funds and collective investment schemes should sustain demand for government securities, supporting auction coverage and secondary-market activity, particularly in 3Q’26 [quarter 3, 2026]. However, the impact may moderate later in the year as increased sovereign and corporate issuance absorbs excess liquidity”, it stated. It also expects the Treasury to progressively build on its return to the domestic bond market through targeted medium- and long-term issuances, supporting yield-curve development and reducing reliance on short-dated T-bills. According to the financial market research firm, this should be complemented by planned debt-reprofiling and bond-buyback operations aimed at retiring high-cost obligations and smoothing the maturity profile. Therefore, issuance should remain active as the government builds the Sinking Fund from GH¢15.6 billion towards its GH¢30 billion year-end target and strengthens buffers ahead of sizeable DDEP maturities from 2027. Investor demand remained robust in the first-half of 2026, with total bids rising 94.1% year-on-year to GH¢234.86 billion. Average target-cover and bid-to-cover ratios of 1.10x and 1.39x, respectively, reflected healthy auction demand despite intermittent moderation in participation.

Dans une lettre adressée au chef de l’État début septembre, et rendue publique en fin de semaine dernière, elles demandent d’amplifier les efforts pour lutter contre les feux de forêts qui ravagent la Grande Île. items.title: What is left of Maspero after national broadcaster’s debt-for-assets swap?
items.description: The National Broadcasting Authority — known by the name of its Downtown headquarters, Maspero — has been weighed down by debt for decades, borrowing heavily from the National Investment Bank (NIB) as it has struggled to maintain a leading role as state broadcaster and production house in a changing media scene, grappling initially with the move to satellite, and now to digital media. All of that accumulated debt, worth a total of around LE139.7 billion, was settled at the end of August, in a single assets-for-debt swap, with the Planning Ministry announcing that the ownership of 44 assets, unused by the broadcasting authority and worth around LE18.06 billion, including land and buildings, would be transferred to the NIB. What the assets are, how they were valued and what will happen to them going forward remains unclear. While sources speaking to Mada Masr pointed to some of the land assets that are owned by the company and indicated some of those included in the deal, they were not aware of how these lands will be leveraged for investment going forward. The move, however, eliminates debts that Maspero has been racking up since the 1980s as the state has, simultaneously, withdrawn its investments from its traditional media vehicles and focused instead on United Media Services (UMS). The ministry has said that the step was taken in line with a broader move to resolve the historical debts of government entities and authorities, part of what it called “the political leadership’s directives.” In this light, the Maspero debt-for-assets swap marks a major step toward implementation of plans the prime minister announced at the beginning of the year to resolve the huge amount of government debt, leveraging state assets and land for investment to write off public borrowing as part of the continuing process of shaping President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s “New Republic.” How was the deal announced? The swap was announced on August 26 as part of a framework agreement signed by the Finance and Planning Ministers, with the heads of NIB and Maspero. The Cabinet initially announced that the total debts were LE88.3 billion, with the Planning Ministry elaborating the following day to state that the total debts resolved amounted to LE139.7 billion, including LE51.4 billion that were written off entirely and that included accumulated interest and late-payment penalties owed by the broadcasting authority. The remaining LE70.24 billion would be repaid by the state, according to the ministry, through the allocation of land to the bank, with the aim of increasing the bank’s asset base and enabling it to redeploy those assets in national projects that would create more jobs — something the ministry referred to as another form of government support for debt settlement. The file was to be fully closed, the Planning Ministry stated, and the accumulation of any new late-payment penalties halted as of July 1 until completion of the settlement procedures. What remains of Maspero? A broadcaster, a senior specialist at the National Broadcasting Authority and a news program director, tell Mada Masr in separate statements that the debt settlement agreement remained unclear and that there was a lack of transparency over how the 44 plots of land belonging to Maspero were valued at LE18 billion. The broadcaster and the director both believe that the government has not disclosed the size or locations of the relinquished land so as not to expose its unfair valuation. According to the broadcaster, who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity, the state allocated vast areas of land to the authority since the launch of state television in the 1960s t o ensure strong transmission coverage in every region, with every governorate having at least one television transmission center. From television’s beginnings until the year 2000, dozens of presidential decrees allocated state land in different governorates for the construction of radio and television transmission stations and transferred them, free of charge, to the Egyptian Radio and Television Union (ETRU) — the entity headquartered at Maspero that would later become the National Broadcasting Authority. According to the news-department director, who spoke to Mada Masr on the condition of anonymity, Maspero owns between 3,000 and 4,500 feddans of land distributed across Sharm el-Sheikh — specifically Umm al-Sid Plateau — the Agouza area and Faisal Street in Giza Governorate, Sharqiya, Minya near Gabel al-Tayr and Zaafarana on the Red Sea coast. It also owns a small plot in the New Capital, the equivalent of no more than three feddans, surrounding a small news studio built out of funding for the capital. The broadcaster added that the authority also owns large areas in Moqattam and Abu Zaabal in Cairo, as well as substantial land in Marsa Matrouh and North and South Sinai. A third source working for a private-sector asset consulting and valuation firm said that one of the most important plots included in the debt settlement is land in Zaafarana formerly owned by the ERTU. Other plots in various areas — including Helwan in Cairo, Fayoum and Upper Egypt — were also part of the agreement. The broadcaster says that information about the settlement also indicates that ownership of radio and television transmission stations would be transferred to the bank, with the exception of the radio and television transmission station in Moqattam, the old media club’s land at the entrance to Moqattam’s upper plateau and the radio building on the Sherifeen Street in the Egyptian Exchange area of Downtown Cairo. According to an informed Housing Ministry source, the studios and staff currently housed in Downtown Cairo’s Maspero building will be moved in full to the new global studios city, planned for the Dahshur area, south of the Giza Plateau. The facility is intended to be used for filming and as a tourist attraction, as part of a project to develop the surroundings of the archaeological Giza Pyramids area. The source says the project was approved by the Cabinet in December 2025 after the international consultancy Wimberly, Allison, Tong & Goo (WATG) was commissioned to prepare its master plan. In its statement on the financial details of the settlement, the Planning Ministry said the inventory process had been conducted with “extreme care” to ensure that no “revenue-generating” assets owned by the authority were affected, in order to preserve its financial position and sustainability. The statement specifically referred to the authority’s shares in satellite operator Nilesat and the Egyptian Media Production City (EMPC), which had already been pledged to the NIB. Those shares are to be fully released once the agreed asset transfers are completed. The government assured that the debt settlement would still allow Maspero to benefit from the returns on its shares in Nilesat and the EMPC. The agreement itself did not specify the worth of the shares, nor the broadcasting authority’s ownership percentage in the two companies. In a subsequent move after the settlement was finalized, the broadcasting authority announced that it owns approximately 40 percent of Nilesat and 45 percent of the EMPC. A quarter century of debt In 2021, the broadcasting authority stated it had not received any loans from the NIB since its establishment, explaining that any debts owed to the bank were not incurred by the authority itself since its creation, but were debts that had been transferred to it when it replaced the former ERTU. Those debts included LE9.6 billion in loans from the NIB, dating back to 1981, on which interest had reached LE32.9 billion by then, bringing total accumulated debt to LE42.6 billion. So, how did the ERTU become so mired in debt? “Maspero was deliberately drowned in debt over the years,” the broadcaster says. She describes a decline in the credibility of state television after the 20 11 revolution, which resulted from the misguided policies of successive administrations, she says, and coincided with the rise of UMS as an alternative, depriving Maspero of its audience, and, consequently, its ability to generate revenue and self-finance. Maspero’s debts began to accumulate when Safwat al-Sherif became Information Minister in 1982. During the tenures of Sherif and Anas al-Fekky, television underwent massive expansion, including the launch of Nilesat, the establishment of the EMPC, the creation of dozens of specialized and regional channels and the modernization of studios and purchase of equipment. Most of these expansions and investment needs were financed through loans from the NIB, at a time when Egyptian television enjoyed significant institutional prestige, and, according to the broadcaster, when no one dared interfere with it. Indicating the decree of expansion, the broadcaster notes that during this period, the number of employees at the ERTU expanded to between 40,000 and 45,000, causing annual wage and pension costs to surpass LE2.5 billion. At the same time, Maspero’s revenues declined as the satellite television market was liberalized and private channels expanded from the beginning of the new millennium. A large share of advertisers and viewers shifted to competing channels, reducing Maspero’s share in the advertising market. Maspero’s production sector, alongside Sono Cairo and the EMPC, used to enjoy a role as the backbone of Egyptian drama from the 1960s until 2010, when Egyptian television produced, financed and broadcast its own works. But the ERTU’s financial collapse and mounting debts to the NIB gradually deprived it of its ability to finance production. As documented by the Central Auditing Organization in a 2016 report , ETRU contracted work out to executive producers and co-producers, financing productions for third parties despite owning the studios and personnel, until its production sector stopped producing television series altogether in 2016. Private production companies and Gulf channels initially filled the gap. Since 2018, however, the role has been assumed by UMS, which acquired major production arms, including Synergy and Media Hub, among others, as well as broadcasting channels such as ONtv, DMC network and Al-Hayah. It consequently came to dominate the production and distribution of the majority of Ramadan television series, while Maspero shifted from being a producer to merely a broadcaster that acquired UMS’s productions under broadcast agreements. The broadcaster explains that in recent years, the drama and programming production role previously performed by Maspero specifically shifted to UMS, which is owned by sovereign entities through The Sovereign Fund of Egypt and Eagle Capital for Financial Investments, a private equity fund owned by the General Intelligence Services. The company now produces a vast array of content and broadcasts these on a variety of channels that are able to operate as private sector companies. Maspero’s role in news also gradually diminished. Since UMS’s acquisition of most private media outlets in Egypt in 2019, the company — through eXtra News, which came under its control, and then Al-Qahera News, launched in November 2022 — has become the state’s de-facto news arm. Meanwhile, Maspero’s Nile News channel, a part of its news sector, has been reduced to broadcasting conventional bulletins and official coverage, without a field correspondent network or modern production resources. Maspero, therefore, no longer earned revenues from producing drama, exclusive broadcasting or radio rights for certain sporting events, particularly as state investment became concentrated in UMS. The director in Maspero’s news sector, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, says Maspero had been stripped of the revenues from sports broadcasting rights, which had generated substantial income, even though matches continued to be broadcast on its channels. “We do not know how UMS acquired the broadcasting rights or under what agreement,” they say. Egyptian television was the exclusive broadcaster of Egyptian Premier League matches until mid-2017. Its last major contract with the Egyptian Football Association, signed in January 2014, was worth LE70 million per season. In the 2017/18 season, the rights passed to Presentation Sports Agency, which took over marketing rights for the league, the Egypt Cup and s major clubs, and assigned broadcasting to ON Sport channels. The entire system then passed to the UMS in 2019 through ON Time Sports, and Maspero exited the sports broadcasting market entirely. Rights values have since risen far beyond the value of Maspero’s contracts. The Egyptian Professional Football Clubs Association announced in June 2026 that broadcasting and commercial rights contracts had increased by 300 percent over four seasons, with the new revenue and prize package reaching LE1 billion, while the value of UMS’ own contracts remained officially undisclosed. The director added that the National Broadcasting Authority’s remaining resources had become almost symbolic, consisting mainly of government advertising and awareness campaigns supposedly intended for state television, as well as radio car licensing fees that the Interior Ministry is expected to remit to the authority. Owners of cars equipped with electronic or entertainment systems pay an annual fee of LE100, 40 percent of which is allocated to the broadcasting authority — a charge commonly known in the media as the “radio tax.” As the broadcasting authority’s installments continued to go unpaid, interest and late-payment penalties accumulated on the principal debt over the years. In the August settlement, the Planning Ministry stated that approximately LE51.4 billion in interest and late-payment penalties was written off, including LE45 billion in late-payment penalties and LE6.4 billion in interest. Interest and penalties therefore accounted for a substantial share of the total debt, rather than the loans’ principal alone. In addition to the debt burden, reports issued by the Central Auditing Organization over the years documented financial and administrative violations, as well as shortcomings in the management and use of some assets owned by the ERTU, that were estimated to be worth billions of Egyptian pounds before some of them were transferred to the National Broadcasting Authority. Both the broadcaster and the news director say that instead of addressing the process through which Maspero was saddled with debt, and reforming it administratively by making use of its assets, the authority was being stripped of those assets. This has raised concerns among employees that new debts could accumulate and eventually lead to the complete liquidation of the authority’s role. Economic advisor and capital markets expert Wael al-Nahhas supports the sources’ view. He describes the Maspero debt settlement as tantamount to liquidating the institution, saying that with Maspero’s resources depleted and its real estate assets stripped away, its continued existence is merely a matter of time. Nahhas says that in 2015, he had worked with officials inside state agencies on a plan to settle Maspero’s debts by investing its assets in a way that would ensure sustainable revenues and keep it functioning. The broadcaster explains that in recent years, the drama and programming production role previously performed by Maspero specifically shifted to UMS, which is owned by sovereign entities through The Sovereign Fund of Egypt and Eagle Capital for Financial Investments, a private equity fund owned by the General Intelligence Services. The company now produces a vast array of content and broadcasts these on a variety of channels that are able to operate as private sector companies. Maspero’s role in news also gradually diminished. Since UMS’s acquisition of most private media outlets in Egypt in 2019, the company — through eXtra News, which came under its control, and then Al-Qahera News, launched in November 2022 — has become the state’s de-facto news arm. Meanwhile, Maspero’s Nile News channel, a part of its news sector, has been reduced to broadcasting conventional bulletins and official coverage, without a field correspondent network or modern production resources. Maspero, therefore, no longer earned revenues from producing drama, exclusive broadcasting or radio rights for certain sporting events, particularly as state investment became concentrated in UMS. The director in Maspero’s news sector, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, says Maspero had been stripped of the revenues from sports broadcasting rights, which had generated substantial income, even though matches continued to be broadcast on its channels. “We do not know how UMS acquired the broadcasting rights or under what agreement,” they say. Egyptian television was the exclusive broadcaster of Egyptian Premier League matches until mid-2017. Its last major contract with the Egyptian Football Association, signed in January 2014, was worth LE70 million per season. In the 2017/18 season, the rights passed to Presentation Sports Agency, which took over marketing rights for the league, the Egypt Cup and s major clubs, and assigned broadcasting to ON Sport channels. The entire system then passed to the UMS in 2019 through ON Time Sports, and Maspero exited the sports broadcasting market entirely. Rights values have since risen far beyond the value of Maspero’s contracts. The Egyptian Professional Football Clubs Association announced in June 2026 that broadcasting and commercial rights contracts had increased by 300 percent over four seasons, with the new revenue and prize package reaching LE1 billion, while the value of UMS’ own contracts remained officially undisclosed. The director added that the National Broadcasting Authority’s remaining resources had become almost symbolic, consisting mainly of government advertising and awareness campaigns supposedly intended for state television, as well as radio car licensing fees that the Interior Ministry is expected to remit to the authority. Owners of cars equipped with electronic or entertainment systems pay an annual fee of LE100, 40 percent of which is allocated to the broadcasting authority — a charge commonly known in the media as the “radio tax.” As the broadcasting authority’s installments continued to go unpaid, interest and late-payment penalties accumulated on the principal debt over the years. In the August settlement, the Planning Ministry stated that approximately LE51.4 billion in interest and late-payment penalties was written off, including LE45 billion in late-payment penalties and LE6.4 billion in interest. Interest and penalties therefore accounted for a substantial share of the total debt, rather than the loans’ principal alone. In addition to the debt burden, reports issued by the Central Auditing Organization over the years documented financial and administrative violations, as well as shortcomings in the management and use of some assets owned by the ERTU, that were estimated to be worth billions of Egyptian pounds before some of them were transferred to the National Broadcasting Authority. Both the broadcaster and the news director say that instead of addressing the process through which Maspero was saddled with debt, and reforming it administratively by making use of its assets, the authority was being stripped of those assets. This has raised concerns among employees that new debts could accumulate and eventually lead to the complete liquidation of the authority’s role. Economic advisor and capital markets expert Wael al-Nahhas supports the sources’ view. He describes the Maspero debt settlement as tantamount to liquidating the institution, saying that with Maspero’s resources depleted and its real estate assets stripped away, its continued existence is merely a matter of time. Nahhas says that in 2015, he had worked with officials inside state agencies on a plan to settle Maspero’s debts by investing its assets in a way that would ensure sustainable revenues and keep it functioning. He explains that it involved using Maspero’s land in prime locations to build world-class studios that could be rented to international news agencies, alongside media projects that would generate income, enabling it to develop its resources and continue operating. The plan, however, ran into laws prohibiting the disposal of land designated for public benefit. Nahhas points out that the settlement recently announced by the government is based on stripping Maspero — and other state institutions indebted to the NIB — of their real estate assets so that the government can continue borrowing. He said that Maspero needs approximately LE20 billion annually, at least, to continue its activities, but that it receives only enough to cover employee salaries from the state budget, which the director and media professional estimate to be around LE220 million per month. Its continued operation amid such scarce resources is therefore “impossible.” According to the broadcaster, Maspero’s workforce has shrunk from 42,000 employees since 2010 to just 15,000 today, after between 60 and 70 percent of its employees retired. She said the average age of current employees is around 50 and expect the next step to be, once outstanding end-of-service payments and financial differences are settled, the introduction of an early-retirement scheme at age 55. She believes this would be welcomed by a large proportion of employees who were replaced by the UMS staff when the company supervised work in the news sector in recent years. The broadcaster and news director said Maspero employees had been told that the deal would be followed by progress on delayed end-of-service benefits and pension payments. Between 6,000 and 7,000 retirees reportedly have unpaid entitlements dating back to 2019, while current employees’ salaries have been frozen since 2014 and bonuses have gone unpaid for approximately 70 months. Debt write-offs in exchange for assets Ten days before the Maspero debt settlement agreement was signed, the NIB’s board announced what it called an “unprecedented financial breakthrough,” recording a net profit of LE6 billion in the fiscal year ending June 2025, compared with losses of LE31.7 billion in the previous year. The bank attributed the turnaround to “progress achieved in resolving financial entanglements with government entities,” pointing to the signing of two framework agreements in June, to settle historic debts dating back to the 1980s worth more than LE196 billion. These settlements covered companies affiliated with the Holding Company for Water and Waste Water and the General Authority for Reconstruction Projects and Agricultural Development. The board also discussed ongoing steps to finalize additional settlements with other government entities and resolve the remaining debts. The two agreements preceding the Maspero settlement were not accompanied by any explanation of their details or the nature of the assets, which, according to multiple Planning Ministry sources, were transferred as part of the debt settlements to the NIB. The NIB is a state-owned bank established by former President Anwar al-Sadat in 1980 and affiliated with the Planning Ministry. It is not a commercial bank: it does not open accounts for individuals or provide conventional banking services. Rather, it is a sovereign financing institution tasked with funding investment projects included in the state’s economic and social development plan. Historically, the bank relied on surpluses from social insurance and pension funds, postal savings funds, proceeds from investment certificates and government bonds, and other resources determined by the state. It directed these funds toward financing projects run by economic authorities and government entities, provided concessional loans for national projects and monitored their implementation and the management of their assets. In recent years, particularly since 2019, the bank has undergone restructuring, including the settlement of its debts with the National Organization for Social Insurance and the Finance Ministry, as well as amendments to its governing law. These changes have paved the way for a gradual shift toward a more investment-oriented role focused on managing portfolios, assets and funds rather than primarily providing loans. A Planning Ministry source describes the process of resolving financial entanglements among government entities as “economic correction, the revival of uncollectible debts — that is, debts unlikely to be repaid — and the provision of assets for investment funds that are expected to be announced soon.” The source stresses that some of the land included in the settlements had already been assigned for management to the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority, and that the government has, for years, been inventorying unused assets belonging to ministries, institutions and government authorities to find ways to assign them to profitable projects. The accumulation of domestic debt — the total amount borrowed in local currency by the government, economic authorities and public entities from within the national economy — is linked to the expansion of state spending and growing financing needs. Its trajectory, however, has accelerated upward since 2011, alongside widening budget deficits and declining sources of revenue. Domestic debt stood at approximately between LE800 and LE900 billion before 2011, exceeded LE2 trillion by 2015 and approached LE4 trillion in 2019, before continuing to rise in subsequent years amid increasing financing needs, higher interest rates and the depreciation of the local currency. By 2025, domestic debt had exceeded LE12 trillion, representing a high proportion of GDP. The bulk of domestic debt consists of government debt instruments, particularly treasury bills and bonds subscribed to by the banking sector and local investors, alongside intergovernmental balances and debts, including the government’s debt to the NIB. Its main problems include the high debt-servicing costs, as interest payments consume a large share of public spending, limiting the resources available for other sectors and services. Deficit and debt financing can also have inflationary effects, particularly when it involves monetary expansion or direct financing by the central bank. Another challenge is the potential crowding out of the private sector, as rising government financing needs may absorb a larger share of the liquidity available in the banking system, limiting financing for private and productive investment. The Planning Ministry source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, explains the government’s decision to disclose some details of the Maspero debt settlement — unlike other debt settlements that have taken place — by pointing to the controversy sparked by businessman Hassan Heikal’s statement, which he describes as the “minor swap.” Heikal, a member of the Cabinet’s advisory Macroeconomic Committee, revived on August 29 a proposal he had first floated at the end of 2025 to eliminate domestic public debt by debt-for-asset swaps, an idea that became known in the media as the “great trade-off.” His idea, published on his personal X account, included transferring ownership of the Suez Canal to the central bank in exchange for settling an equivalent amount of Finance Ministry debts. Explaining his proposal again in light of the Maspero debt-swap, Heikal said : “Maspero cleared its debts and is capable of spending on programs and content. The National Investment Bank took assets equivalent to the debt and will develop and operate them.” He added: “Remove the word ‘Maspero’ and replace it with ‘the state’; remove ‘National Investment Bank’ and replace it with ‘the central bank’; remove ‘land’ and replace it with ownership stakes in state-owned companies or even the Suez Canal — and that amounts to eliminating domestic public debt.” These ideas sparked widespread public anger over fears that sovereign state assets, such as the Suez Canal, could be relinquished from sovereign control and sold off to investors, particularly amid growing Gulf investor interest in Egyptian assets. items.title: Diphtérie : 11 décès dus à l’épidémie
items.description: Au total, 11 décès ont été enregistrés le 20 septembre à travers les 31 districts sanitaires, touchés par la diphtérie. C’est ce qui ressort du point fait lundi par le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique. Onze décès ont été causés par l’épidémie de la diphtérie depuis le 1er août, date à laquelle le premier cas est apparu. Le point de la situation au 20 septembre fait état de 114 cas qui ont été confirmés à travers les 31 districts sanitaires répartis dans 12 régions. La région de Kédougou compte 33 cas (kédougou 23, Saraya 8 et Salémata 2 cas), Louga 16 cas (kébémer 6, Darou-Mousty 8, Sakal et Louga chacun 1 cas) et Dakar 15 cas (Guédiawaye 7, Keur Massar 3 et Dakar-Ouest, Dakar-Nord, Dakar-Sud, Pikine et Sangalkam chacun 1 cas). Sous la barre des 15 cas : la région de Thiès a enregistré 12 cas (Mbour 11 et Thiadiaye 1 cas), Diourbel 13 cas (Touba 12 et Mbacké 1 cas) et Matam 6 cas (le département de Matam 5 et Thilogne 1 cas). A lire aussi : Diphtérie au Sénégal : le bilan grimpe à 57 cas confirmés et 8 décès, Kédougou toujours en première ligne L’épidémie a infecté 5 personnes à Kaolack (Kaolack 1, Guinguinéo 2 et Ndoffane 2 cas) et Tambacounda compte également 5 cas confirmés (dont 4 à Bakel et 1 à Diankhé-makha). Le ministère de la Santé a déclaré 4 cas à Kolda (les 4 à Vélingara), 2 cas à Saint-Louis (1 à Saint-Louis et l’autre à Dagana), 2 cas à Ziguinchor (répartis entre Bignona et Ziguinchor) et 1 cas à Fatick. Le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique rappelle que la « diphtérie est une maladie infectieuse et contagieuse mais évitable grâce à la vaccination ». Il invite ainsi les parents à respecter le calendrier vaccinal du Programme élargi de vaccination. L’épidémie peut se manifester entre autres par un mal de gorge, de la fièvre, une difficulté à avaler, un enrouement et un gonflement du cou. La diphtérie peut aussi entraîner la présence de membranes grisâtres dans la gorge, causant des difficultés respiratoires. Boubacar DIOP (Stagiaire)

items.title: De la cocaïne cachée dans deux camions citernes saisie à Tamanrasset
items.description: Une importante quantité de cocaïne a été saisie ce lundi par les forces de l’ANP à Tamanrasset dans l’extrême sud du pays, a annoncé le ministère de la Défense nationale dans un communiqué. Deux narcotrafiquants ont été arrêtés lors de cette opération. « Dans le cadre des efforts continus déployés pour sécuriser les frontières nationales et lutter contre les barons de la contrebande et le crime organisé, et grâce à une utilisation optimale du renseignement, des détachements conjoints de l'Armée nationale populaire du secteur militaire de Tamanrasset ont réussi ce lundi 21 septembre 2026 à arrêter deux trafiquants de drogue et à saisir une importante quantité de cocaïne, estimée à plus de 58 kilogrammes », a indiqué le MDN. La cocaïne était cachée dans deux camions citernes La cocaïne était « soigneusement dissimulée dans deux camions citernes », a précisé la même source. « Cette opération confirme la pleine capacité opérationnelle de toutes les composantes de l'Armée nationale populaire à faire face à toute tentative d'inonder le pays de stupéfiants et de porter atteinte à la sécurité des citoyens », a conclu le MDN. L’Algérie a décidé de créer un organisme sécuritaire spécialisé dans la lutte contre le trafic de drogue sur le modèle de la DEA américaine, et de transformer une caserne militaire dans le désert de Tanezrouft en prison de haute sécurité pour les narcotrafiquants. L’article De la cocaïne cachée dans deux camions citernes saisie à Tamanrasset est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Rentrée scolaire 2026 : l’Intersyndicale de l’éducation pose ses conditions avant tout recrutement
items.description: L’Intersyndicale de l’éducation, composée du Syndicat national de l’éducation (SNE), du Syndicat libre des enseignants-chercheurs de Guinée (SLECG) et de la Fédération syndicale des professionnels de l’éducation (FSPE), a animé un point de presse ce lundi 21 septembre à Dixinn. Au cœur des échanges : le recrutement des enseignants annoncé par le ministère de la Fonction publique, le protocole d’accord signé le 3 janvier 2026 et les préalables que les syndicats estiment indispensables à l’organisation d’un concours et à une rentrée scolaire apaisée. Le secrétaire général du SNE, Michel Pépé Balamou, a d’abord tenu à clarifier la position de l’Intersyndicale sur le principe d’un concours. « L’Intersyndicale que vous voyez n’est pas opposée à l’organisation d’un concours. Il faut que cela soit très clair. Parce que c’est ce qui se dit actuellement dans la cité : “Les syndicalistes veulent que n’importe qui soit en classe pour enseigner nos enfants, ils s’opposent au concours”. Non ! Ni le SLECG, ni la FSPE, ni le SNE, personne n’est opposé à ce que les meilleurs soient recrutés pour enseigner dans les écoles de la République », a-t-il déclaré. Selon le responsable syndical, l’exigence de l’Intersyndicale porte avant tout sur le respect du protocole d’accord conclu avec le gouvernement. 4 500 enseignants ayant la moyenne revendiqués Michel Pépé Balamou rappelle qu’en 2024, 14 500 enseignants contractuels communaux avaient été identifiés, recensés, biométrisés puis soumis à une évaluation en pratique de classe. À l’issue de cette évaluation, 10 000 enseignants ont été retenus et 4 500 recalés, selon les chiffres avancés par le secrétaire général du SNE. Il précise toutefois que la majorité des 4 500 candidats recalés auraient obtenu la moyenne. « Parmi ces 4 500, seuls 60 n’ont pas eu la moyenne (…) Tout le reste, plus de 4 400 personnes ont obtenu une moyenne égale ou supérieure à 10/20. Cela signifie qu’ils ont le niveau », a-t-il soutenu. Pour le syndicaliste, le protocole d’accord leur accorde une priorité à l’engagement. « Le français est très clair : prioritaires à l’engagement. Qu’est-ce que cela signifie ? Cela implique que nous devions prendre leur moyenne : tous ceux qui ont entre 10 et 20/20 n’ont plus de concours à passer », a-t-il affirmé. Il estime donc que les enseignants contractuels de la zone spéciale de Conakry devraient, eux, être soumis à une évaluation en pratique de classe, conformément au protocole. Des retards dans l’application du protocole L’Intersyndicale reconnaît que certaines dispositions financières du protocole ont été appliquées. « En fin de septembre, 1 200 000 GNF doivent être ajoutés à la prime de documentation (pour la porter à 1 500 000 GNF), et 200 000 GNF restent au titre des indemnités de logement et de transport. C’est donc 1 400 000 GNF qui doivent être intégrés au salaire de tous les enseignants de Guinée à la fin de ce mois. Sur ce volet financier, le protocole est respecté », a expliqué Michel Pépé Balamou. En revanche, il déplore le retard accusé dans la mise en œuvre de plusieurs dispositions techniques. Selon lui, le protocole signé le 3 janvier 2026 prévoyait notamment la mise en place, dès février, de plusieurs commissions techniques. Celles-ci n’auraient finalement été installées qu’en avril, après des menaces syndicales. Trois commissions sont notamment concernées : celle chargée des enseignants contractuels communaux non retenus à l’issue des évaluations, celle chargée des actes de nomination des cadres devant bénéficier des primes de fonction et celle consacrée à la révision du statut particulier des personnels de l’éducation et de la formation. L’Intersyndicale fixe ses préalables Pour l’Intersyndicale, plusieurs engagements doivent être satisfaits avant l’organisation de tout concours au niveau du ministère de l’Éducation nationale. Elle réclame notamment : l’engagement des 4 500 enseignants contractuels communaux ayant obtenu la moyenne ; l’engagement des près de 2 000 enseignants contractuels de Conakry ; le paiement des 9 mois d’arriérés de salaire des 10 000 enseignants des collectivités ; la régularisation des situations administratives, notamment les échelons, indices et reclassements ; la régularisation des primes d’incitation, particulièrement en zone rurale ; l’amélioration des conditions matérielles et financières dans les établissements scolaires, notamment les écoles délabrées, le manque de latrines, d’eau, de tables-bancs, de matériel didactique et de cahiers. « Nous n’accepterons aucun principe d’organisation de concours au niveau du Ministère de l’Éducation nationale. L’Intersyndicale reste catégorique et formelle : tant que les points susmentionnés et clairement identifiés dans le protocole d’accord signé le 3 janvier 2026 ne sont pas satisfaits, il n’y aura pas de possibilité d’aboutir à une ouverture apaisée des classes », a conclu Michel Pépé Balamou. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Rentrée scolaire 2026 : l’Intersyndicale de l’éducation pose ses conditions avant tout recrutement est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Lutte TV Awards 2026 : le ministère des Sports dément tout « manque de considération » et pointe une invitation informelle
items.description: Deux jours après la cérémonie des Lutte TV Awards, le ministère de la Jeunesse et des Sports répond aux critiques sur l'absence de sa ministre. Dans une « mise au point » publiée ce lundi 21 septembre 2026, il affirme n'avoir reçu aucune invitation officielle et renvoie la responsabilité aux organisateurs. La cérémonie s'est tenue le samedi 19 septembre au NOOM Hôtel de Dakar. L'absence de la ministre y avait suscité des critiques, certaines dénonçant un désintérêt pour le monde de la lutte. Le ministère y répond en évoquant des « allégations publiques » et « un prétendu manque de considération envers le secteur de la lutte ». « Aucune invitation officielle » Le ministère est catégorique : la ministre « n'a reçu aucune invitation officielle à cet événement par les voies institutionnelles ». Il va plus loin en citant les organisateurs, qui auraient « eux-mêmes reconnu n'avoir sollicité le Ministère qu'à 48 heures de la cérémonie, par un canal informel ». Selon le communiqué, ce contact tardif s'expliquait par « les incertitudes qui pesaient sur la tenue de l'événement ». Le ministère en tire la conclusion suivante : « aucune participation ne pouvait raisonnablement être programmée ». Un rappel au « cadre de gouvernance du sport » Le texte prend ensuite un ton plus ferme. Le ministère rappelle « l'exigence du respect du cadre de gouvernance du sport, notamment dans leurs rapports avec l'administration ». Il lance aussi « un appel à la responsabilité dans les prises de parole publiques, surtout de la part de personnes citées en modèle », sans désigner nommément qui que ce soit. Le département assure qu'il « s’emploie au développement de toutes les disciplines sportives, sans distinction » et « réaffirme son engagement constant aux côtés de la lutte, sport national et patrimoine de notre pays ». Il conclut que « les manquements des acteurs ne sauraient être couverts par la désinformation et la manipulation ». O.B.N

items.description: Black Stars head coach Carlos Queiroz says the decision to replace Mohammed Kudus in the squad is to allow the player become fully fit. Kudus, who has as initially included in the 24-man squad list for the upcoming game against Côte d’Ivoire, Gambia and Morocco. However, the Tottenham Hotspur midfielder communicated his decision to withdraw from squad with his place being taken by Mohammed Fuseini. Speaking at Monday afternoon’s press conference, the Portuguese trainer said the player needed more time to recover fully after his engagement against Aston Villa. “It is simple for you guys to understand.
